Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify appropriate indications for the surgical management of cavovarus foot deformity.
Understand the difference between joint-sparing and arthrodesis procedures.
Identify appropriate soft-tissue procedures for specific contractures and deformities.
Differentiate and understand appropriate forefoot and hindfoot bony procedures to manage
respective deformities.
Understand the risks associated with surgical management and postoperative complications.

Pain, instability, deformity, and skin breakdown are the primary surgical indications in patients
with a cavovarus foot.
In most patients, nonsurgical treatment should be attempted before surgical treatment. Skin
breakdown may be an exception to this.
Surgical management is considered if deformity progression causes symptoms or muscle
weakness results in progressive contractures of the affected joint and antagonistic muscle
units.
Arthritis generally is an indication for arthrodesis.
Earlier surgical management may allow for correction of a flexible deformity before it becomes
rigid.
Most adult patients require some form of osseous surgical treatment in addition to soft-tissue
procedures.
In general, no standard criteria for specific procedures exist, and each patient’s treatment plan
must be individually tailored (Resource 1; Figure 1).

Inability to comply with postoperative protocols

Surgical Planning and Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Thorough patient history and physical examination
Detailed assessment of deformity and disability
Evaluation of rigid versus flexible deformity
Weight-bearing radiographs of the foot, ankle, and hindfoot
Advanced imaging studies as appropriate: CT, MRI, weight-bearing CT

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning for deformity correction should include a detailed patient history
and physical examination. This should include evaluation of gait and weight-bearing
alignment of the feet and the lower extremities. Increased external tibial torsion is
common in patients with a cavovarus foot deformity. The neurologic examination should
include assessment of sensation, motor strength, reflexes, and intrinsic wasting
(including of the hands). Muscle strength should be assessed and compared with that of
the contralateral side. The skin should be evaluated for ulceration and callus formation.
Pedal pulses should be palpated. If absent, vascular testing or consultation should be
ordered. Ankle stability must be evaluated. The presence of forefoot driven hindfoot
varus is assessed via the Coleman block test. Importantly, the flexibility/rigidity of the
deformity must be carefully assessed to guide surgical management.
Imaging studies should include weight-bearing radiographs of the foot and ankle and a
hindfoot alignment radiograph.1 Preoperatively, CT and MRI aid in evaluating bone stock
or soft-tissue integrity, respectively, and may guide surgical decision making. Weight-
bearing CT is becoming increasingly available, and affords excellent three-dimensional
analysis of bony anatomy and alignment, helping to better understand the deformity
under physiologic load.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:36 AM

Patient Positioning/Approach
The patient is routinely placed in the supine position.
Fluoroscopy should be available, and usually a mini C-arm will suffice.
A thigh tourniquet allows for unrestricted intraoperative assessment of tendon balance.
Multiple, separate incisions often are indicated, related to the selected procedures (Resource
2; Figure 2)
Extensile incisions should be used if possible.
Figure 2
Illustration of a foot and ankle shows approaches for lateral ligament reconstruction and subtle
cavus foot correction. Incision one (1) is used to achieve reconstruction of the lateral ligament.
Incision one also affords access to the peroneal tendons should peroneal tendon transfer be
required. Incision two (2) is used to achieve a lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy. Incision three (3)
affords access to the base of the first metatarsal should dorsiflexion osteotomy be required.
(Reproduced from Deben SE, Pomeroy GC: Subtle cavus foot: Diagnosis and management. J Am
Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[8]:512-520.)
Surgical Procedures
Soft-Tissue Procedures
SEND FEEDBACK

Plantar Fascia Release
Release of the plantar fascia is used to lessen first metatarsal plantar flexion, and thereby
address the cavus deformity.
Tendon Lengthening
Posterior tibial tendon lengthening or release (as in cases of tendon transfer) may aid in
correcting medial peritalar subluxation and hindfoot varus.
Flexor digitorum longus lengthening or release may further aid in correction of varus
deformity and also may aid in the release of some contracture in patients with claw toes.
Achilles tendon/gastrocnemius lengthening may be necessary but should be considered
carefully in patients with a calcaneus deformity.
Apparent equinus may be secondary to proximal joint contractures, specifically the knee and
hip.
Posteromedial Capsular Structure Release
Capsulotomies of the medial talonavicular and subtalar joints aid in correcting peritalar
subluxation and hindfoot varus. These should not be overlooked, and thorough release is
important.
Ligament Reconstruction
Lateral ankle ligament reconstruction is useful in patients with ankle instability. In patients
with a deformity, lateral ligament reconstruction should not be performed in isolation.

Soft-Tissue Procedures
In some patients with a flexible deformity and in skeletally immature patients, soft-tissue
procedures alone may afford sufficient correction. In patients with a more rigid
deformity, each of the aforementioned procedures may be necessary or valuable to
maintain correction or prevent recurrence.
Plantar fascia release (Steindler procedure) allows for relaxation of the tether between
the heel and plantar flexed first ray and usually is performed near the origin of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:36 AM
AAOS | Cavovarus Foot Deformity: Surgical Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001015
6/21

plantar fascia at the calcaneus. This usually is one of the initial surgical steps. Similarly, a
contracture of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex may prevent deformity correction. In
patients with a varus heel, the posterior structures are effectively shortened, and
gastrocnemius-soleus complex release should be considered early in the procedure.
Determination of the need for Achilles tendon lengthening versus gastrocnemius
recession is made via Silfverskiöld testing. The gastrocnemius often is lengthened via a
medial-based incision, whereas Achilles tendon lengthening can be performed
percutaneously (Hoke triple hemisection) or in an open fashion (Z-lengthening),
depending on the degree of contracture.
The role of contracture of posteromedial structures should not be overlooked. Similar to
the gastrocnemius-soleus complex, contracture of the posterior tibial tendon may
contribute to and prevent deformity correction. If the posterior tibial tendon will not be
needed for transfer, this can be Z-lengthened. If this is insufficient or patients with claw
toes, the flexor digitorum longus tendon can be lengthened through the same incision.
In addition, the posteromedial capsular structures also present static restraint against
deformity correction. An extensive release of the talonavicular and subtalar joints and
the spring ligament may be necessary.
Lateral ligament reconstruction is dependent on patient symptoms but also can be
evaluated via physical examination and via weight-bearing and stress radiographs.
Patients with chronic ankle instability or recurrent ankle sprains may benefit from
augmented ligament repair. In some patients, recurrent instability may be the driving
force for surgical treatment. In these patients, simultaneous correction of the cavovarus
deformity to protect the ligament repair usually is necessary.
Tendon Transfers
Peroneal Tendons
Transferring the peroneus longus to the peroneus brevis eliminates strong plantar flexion of
the first ray and augments ankle eversion/dorsiflexion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:36 AM
AAOS | Cavovarus Foot Deformity: Surgical Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001015
7/21

In long-standing or neglected cases, the peroneal tendons occasionally are irreparable, and
substitution with the flexor hallucis longus or the flexor digitorum longus may be necessary.
Posterior Tibial Tendon
Transfer of the posterior tibial tendon to the dorsum of the foot through the interosseous
membrane decreases the varus moment and may aid in ankle dorsiflexion. This is particularly
helpful in patients with a neurogenic cavovarus deformity who have weakness with
dorsiflexion and eversion.
Claw Toes
Flexor-to-extensor transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor procedure) of the lesser toes is useful in
patients with flexible claw toes; however, given the neuropathic nature of claw toes, proximal
interphalangeal joint fusion in combination with metacarpophalangeal joint release usually is
necessary.
The clawed hallux usually is managed via a Jones procedure, which includes interphalangeal
joint fusion and transfer of the extensor hallucis longus tendon to the first metatarsal neck.

Tendon Transfers
Tendon transfers performed in isolation rarely are sufficient but are an important tool
for deformity correction and balance of forces to maintain alignment. Peroneus longus
to brevis transfer is associated with multiple advantages. Simple release of the peroneus
longus removes the deforming plantar flexion force of the longus on the first metatarsal,
thereby reducing cavus. Subsequent transfer of the longus to the brevis augments
hindfoot eversion, thereby addressing hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction. This
tendon transfer usually is performed in a side-to-side fashion or with the use of a
Pulvertaft weave and can be performed distal to the inferior retinaculum at the lateral
aspect of the foot or proximal to the superior retinaculum above the ankle. This is
dependent on surgeon preference and the location of other necessary surgical incisions.
Compared with lengthening, posterior tibial tendon transfer is more useful for the
management of equinovarus deformity associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:36 AM
AAOS | Cavovarus Foot Deformity: Surgical Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001015
8/21

after cerebrovascular accident because these conditions often lead to weakened tibialis
anterior and peroneus brevis function. The posterior tibial tendon is most commonly
transferred through the interosseous membrane and inserted into the
cuneiforms/cuboid to augment weak dorsiflexion/eversion at the expense of inversion.
In some severe cases of footdrop, this can be anastomosed with the tibial anterior and
peroneus longus (Bridle procedure).
Claw toes are commonly associated with a cavovarus deformity. This is driven by an
imbalance of the intrinsic and extrinsic musculature. On physical examination, they are
exacerbated by ankle dorsiflexion. If claw toes remain flexible, a flexor-to-extensor
transfer may be useful for balancing the deforming forces. If rigid, proximal
interphalangeal fusion and metacarpophalangeal release (including extensor digitorum
longus lengthening) are indicated. A clawed great toe can be managed via arthrodesis of
the interphalangeal joint in combination with transfer of the extensor hallucis longus
tendon to the first metatarsal neck (Jones procedure). This corrects the hallux deformity,
provides a dorsiflexion moment to counteract the deforming forces of the plantar flexed
first ray, and assists with ankle dorsiflexion.
Osseous Correction
Lateralizing Calcaneal Osteotomy
Hindfoot varus is managed via a lateralizing osteotomy of the calcaneus.
This osteotomy also is useful because it corrects the foot during heel strike and lateralizes the
force of the Achilles tendon vector during toe-off.
Overcorrection may create tension on the tarsal tunnel and its contents.

Lateralizing Calcaneal Osteotomy
Calcaneal osteotomy is a mainstay procedure for hindfoot deformity correction. Many
techniques for calcaneal realignment have been described. Calcaneal osteotomies can
be performed in a traditional open fashion with the use of a saw/osteotome or via
newer, minimally invasive techniques with the use of specialized burrs.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:36 AM
AAOS | Cavovarus Foot Deformity: Surgical Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001015
9/21

The two most common types of osteotomy are a laterally based closing wedge
osteotomy (Dwyer) or a straight cut to allow for lateralization and, if desired, dorsal
translation of the calcaneal tuberosity (Resource 3; Figure 3). Note that lateral
translation of the posterior tuberosity of the calcaneus has been shown in vitro and in
vivo to put excess tension on the tarsal tunnel and may result in
parasthesias/neuropathy of the tibial nerve. Prophylactic tarsal tunnel release can be
performed if increased concern for or preexisting nerve symptoms exists. Dorsal shift of
the calcaneal tuberosity helps correct elevated calcaneal pitch and effectively lengthens
the triceps surae (Resource 4; Figure 4). Dorsal shift also may increase load on the base
of the fifth metatarsal because of changes in mechanical foot alignment. These two
procedures also can be combined; specifically, a closing wedge can be simultaneously
translated laterally and dorsally. A more powerful yet technically demanding procedure
is a Z-type osteotomy. This technique allows for multiplanar translation (lateral and
dorsal) and rotation (valgus and abduction) for deformity correction (Figure 5).
Figure 3
Schematic drawings of an ankle show the procedure for a lateral slide calcaneal
osteotomy. A, Lateral view show the posterior lateral incision (A) and placement of the
calcaneal cut with a saw after the soft tissues have been retracted (B). C, Oblique coronal

Oblique coronal (D) and lateral (E) views show the osteotomy held with the use of two

Dorsiflexion Osteotomy/Arthrodesis of the First Metatarsal/First Tarsometatarsal Joint
Dorsal closing wedge osteotomy of the proximal first metatarsal is indicated for flexible or
rigid first metatarsal plantar flexion without adjacent tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint arthritis.
Closing wedge arthrodesis at the first TMT joint is indicated if arthritis is present at this joint.

Dorsiflexion Osteotomy/Arthrodesis of the First Metatarsal/First
Tarsometatarsal Joint
These procedures may be beneficial early in patients with a forefoot driven deformity
that remains flexible and may be sufficient in isolation to allow for hindfoot correction.
These procedures also can be used in patients with a more severe or rigid deformity in
conjunction with other corrective measures as a balancing procedure for the first
metatarsal plantar flexion deformity (Figure 6).
Figure 6
Medial view illustrations of an ankle shows first metatarsal osteotomy for management
of a fixed first metatarsal cavus deformity. A, A plantar flexed first ray with the deformity
in the first metatarsal is shown. The shaded area depicts the wedge to be removed from
the first tarsometatarsal joint. B, The wedge is closed and fixed with the use of a four-

hole, one-quarter tubular plate and 2.7-mm or 3.5-mm cortical screws. C, In an
alternative technique, bone from the proximal metatarsal metaphysis (shaded area) is
removed. Alignment of the foot is corrected in a manner similar to that shown in panel
B. D, Fixation is performed with the use of a two- or three-hole, one-third tubular plate
and 3.5-mm cortical screws. (Adapted with permission from Hansen ST Jr, ed: Functional
Reconstruction of the Foot and Ankle. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams and Wilkins,
2000, p 393.)
Arthrodesis
Used in patients with arthritis or severe/rigid deformity
Subtalar arthrodesis (talocalcaneal joint)
Talonavicular arthrodesis
Calcaneocuboid arthrodesis
Triple arthrodesis combines all three of these procedures

Arthrodesis
Triple arthrodesis is the most powerful arthrodesis procedure for the management of
hindfoot deformity. However, patients undergoing triple arthrodesis may require
forefoot and/or soft-tissue procedures. In addition, a poorly aligned triple arthrodesis
may place excessive stress on the ankle ligaments, resulting in ankle deformity and
arthritis. Subtalar arthrodesis can be performed with a closing wedge at the joint to
optimize correction of heel varus. Talonavicular arthrodesis allows for control of
adduction and pronation of the midfoot/forefoot. Calcaneocuboid arthrodesis acts as a
lateral column shortening procedure to help correct forefoot adduction (Resource 5;
Figure 7).

Midfoot/Lesser Metatarsal Osteotomy
Dorsal/dorsolateral closing wedge osteotomies of the lesser metatarsals
Closing wedge osteotomy of the midfoot through the cuneiforms or TMT joints

Midfoot/Lesser Metatarsal Osteotomy
Multiple closing wedge osteotomies of the lesser metatarsals or a larger osteotomy
through the cuneiforms or TMT joints serves a similar purpose as dorsiflexion osteotomy
of the first ray. This helps to correct plantar flexion and adduction of the

osteotomy/fusion (Figure 8).
Figure 8
Illustrations show midfoot osteotomy to manage midfoot cavus. A, Transverse cross-

via a dorsally based wedge. The cuneiforms are configured as a roman arch, with the

Cast immobilization is required to close the osteotomy and to maintain correction and

Ankle Arthrosis
Concurrent ankle arthritis may warrant management in combination with management of the
deformity.
Supramalleolar osteotomy may suffice for eccentric ankle arthritis.
Ankle arthrodesis or arthroplasty is necessary in patients with global joint involvement.
Postoperative Management
A well-padded plaster splint is routinely applied for the first 2 weeks postoperatively.
At 2 weeks postoperatively, the patient is seen for a wound check, suture removal, and
potential imaging studies.
Patients remain immobilized and non–weight-bearing for 6 to 8 weeks postoperatively or until
sufficient bony union is achieved.
After a stable, plantigrade foot is achieved, some patients will require an orthotic device. This
is particularly common in neuromuscular cases to correct the weakness of the tibialis anterior
muscle. Although tibialis posterior tendon transfer through the interosseous membrane may
restore some degree of active dorsiflexion, it may not be adequate to correct the footdrop. In
these patients, an ankle-foot orthosis may be necessary.
Complications
Nonunion/Malunion
Bony procedures are associated with an inherent risk of nonunion. Risk factors for nonunion
include diabetes mellitus, smoking, noncompliance, poor bone stock, suboptimal surgical
technique, and possibly low vitamin D levels.
Malunion most often is the result of incomplete correction or inadequate internal fixation.
Malalignment

9/3/26, 7:36 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001015
17/21

This may be caused by under-correction or recurrent deformity.
Under-correction may be the result of insufficient soft-tissue releases or bony re-alignment. A
bony procedure without appropriate tendon balancing may lead to recurrent, continued, or
progressive deformity.
Less commonly, malalignment may be to the result of failure to account for other alignment
issues in the limb.
Infection/Wound Healing Complications
Correction of severe deformity may place the medial skin and soft tissues under tension,
leading to dehiscence and infection.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
All major foot and ankle surgery in combination with postoperative immobilization is
associated with an increased risk for deep vein thrombosis.
Routine prophylactic anticoagulation is recommended postoperatively.
More aggressive anticoagulation or preoperative hematologic consultation may be indicated in
patients with a history of thromboembolism.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Care must be taken during dissection to protect the peripheral nerves.
Nerve injury may lead to numbness or painful neuroma.
Depending on the procedures performed, the superficial peroneal, sural, deep peroneal, and
tibial nerves are at risk.
Aggressive correction of hindfoot varus may place tension on the tarsal tunnel. Depending on
the rigidity and severity of the deformity, prophylactic release of the tarsal tunnel should be
considered.
Adjacent Joint Arthrosis
Arthrodesis procedures lead to increased stress on adjacent joints, increasing the likelihood of
arthritis in these joints.
Outcomes


Outcomes
Outcomes in cavovarus foot reconstruction are difficult to quantify because of the
variety of etiologies and procedures performed. Most evidence consists of level III or
level IV studies. Most studies report good outcomes, with improvement in pain and
function.2,3 Residual hindfoot varus is reported in many patients despite surgical
treatment. Overall, patients who undergo corrective surgical treatment for the
management of idiopathic cavovarus have better outcomes than those with
neuromuscular conditions. In addition, patients with ankle arthritis generally have
poorer outcomes. Therefore, ankle arthritis may be a good indication for earlier
correction to normalize contact stresses across the ankle and prevent progression of
arthrosis.4,5 To the knowledge of the authors of this lesson, the longest follow-up
investigation reports on a cohort of patients who have Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with
a mean follow-up of more than 25 years.6 The authors demonstrated overall reasonable
maintenance of correction, with most patients continuing with standard shoe wear. Just
less than one-half of the patients required an in-shoe or ankle-foot orthosis at final
follow-up; however, only five patients (19%) had heel varus measurements within a
normal range at final follow-up.
Overall, cavovarus deformities are heterogeneous, complex, and challenging to manage.
Patients benefit from thoughtful and strategic surgical treatment. Goals may vary on a
case-by-case basis and may range from fitting into normal shoes to returning to sports
activity. This must be carefully considered before surgical management.
